T-01 The inverted instruction ★★★★★

The stem asks for the exception, with NOT, EXCEPT, INCORRECT arriving late in a long sentence, past the point where the eye has begun scanning options.

What is the remedy?
column2: Circle the negation before looking at any option, then consciously restate the task: I am hunting the false one; three of these will be true and I must resist them. Say it internally. Two seconds, and it is the cheapest insurance in the paper.

column1:
T-02 The double negative ★★★☆☆

A negation in the stem and one inside the option — which of the following is not incorrect, or a body not excluded from a provision.

What is the remedy?
column2: Rewrite, do not reason. Cancel the pair in the margin and restate positively in three words. Not incorrect becomes true. Never hold two negations in working memory.

column1:
T-03 The quantified stem — how many of the above are correct ★★★★★

Four statements; options are Only one / Only two / Only three / All four.

What is the remedy?
column2: Adjudicate, then count — never count by feel. Write T, F or ? beside every statement in the booklet, then add up your own marks arithmetically. One ? converts the item from a knowledge question into a probability question, and you should treat it as such rather than letting a sense of the likely total choose for you. The protocol below is the whole of it. ::: check | CHECK YOURSELF · THE THREE-PART COUNT PROTOCOL 1. Adjudicate each statement in isolation, writing T, F or ? physically beside it 2. Never guess the count from a feeling. The count must be arithmetic on your own marks 3. If you have even one ?, treat the question as elimination-only: check whether both candidate counts appear among the options. If they do and the ? will not resolve, this is a genuine probability-sweep question, not a knowledge question — and per F11.1 §1.2 you should still attempt it :::

column1:
T-04 The best-answer question disguised as a correct-answer question ★★★★☆

Two or more options are factually true, but one is more complete or more directly responsive. The stem carries a silent superlative — the principal objective, the most appropriate, or merely the objective.

What is the remedy?
column2: When a second option also looks true, do not resolve by re-checking truth. Resolve by scope matching: re-read the stem, fix its exact scope, and take the option whose scope is identical — neither broader nor narrower.

column1:
T-05 Scope creep in the stem ★★★★☆

A familiar fact wrapped in a slightly widened scope — in all States and Union Territories, for every establishment, throughout India, since inception.

What is the remedy?
column2: Underline every scope word, then ask one question of each: is there a known exception? If yes, the option is false.

column1:
T-06 The pair-count matching question ★★★★★

Consider the following pairs. How many pairs are correctly matched? — typically Act and year, scheme and ministry, committee and subject, Article and content.

What is the remedy?
column2: Adjudicate in order of your confidence, not the printed order. Resolve the certain pairs first; that often fixes the count without the obscure pair mattering at all. If it does not, prefer the count that requires the famous-but-subtly-wrong pair to be wrong — that is the pair the question was built around.

column1:
T-07 Absolute qualifiers in the options ★★★★★

always, never, only, all, none, must, invariably, in no case, cannot.

What is the remedy?
column2: The highest-yield elimination heuristic available: absolutes are false far more often than true, because Indian statutory reality is built of provisos and exemptions. When an option says only or never, spend your effort constructing one counter-example; find it and you have a hard elimination. ::: trap | TRAP · DO NOT LET T-07 BECOME SUPERSTITION Absolutes are true where the statute itself is absolute. A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. Article 360 has never been invoked. Under the EPF & MP Act, an establishment once covered continues to be covered even if strength falls below the threshold. Use the heuristic to direct suspicion, never to decide alone. An elimination made on the presence of the word never, with no supporting fact, is a soft elimination wearing a hard elimination's clothes — exactly the failure §1.2 warns about. :::

column1:
T-08 Hedged qualifiers in the options ★★★★☆

The mirror image — generally, usually, may, often, some, ordinarily, tends to.

What is the remedy?
column2: Never eliminate an option merely for being cautious. Forced to choose between an absolute and a hedged option with no other basis, take the hedged one.

column1:
T-09 The near-miss number ★★★★★

The correct figure with one digit, one order of magnitude, or one adjacent statutory value changed.

What is the remedy?
column2: §5's numbers ledger, and one habit: when a number appears, do not ask does this look right. Ask which slot does this number belong to. Recognition without slot-assignment is precisely what the trap eats.

column1:
T-10 Section and Article number swaps ★★★★★

Correct content attached to the wrong Article, Section, Schedule or Chapter.

What is the remedy?
column2: Learn numbers in clusters with a narrative, never as isolated pairs. The Directive Principles on labour run as a story — 39 health and strength of workers, 41 right to work and public assistance, 42 just and humane conditions and maternity relief, 43 living wage, 43A workers' participation. Rehearse the run, not the pairs.

column1:
T-11 Act name and year swaps ★★★★☆



What is the remedy?
column2: A recitable chronology makes a year-swap visible instantly. Workmen's Compensation 1923, Trade Unions 1926, Payment of Wages 1936, Standing Orders 1946, Industrial Disputes 1947, Minimum Wages 1948, ESI 1948, EPF & MP 1952, Maternity Benefit 1961, Payment of Bonus 1965, Contract Labour 1970, Payment of Gratuity 1972, Equal Remuneration 1976, EDLI Scheme 1976, Unorganised Workers' Social Security 2008 — then the Codes: Wages 2019, and Industrial Relations, Social Security, and OSH & WC all 2020.

column1:
T-12 The category swap — constitutional, statutory, executive ★★★★★

A body given the wrong legal pedigree. EPFO's Central Board of Trustees called constitutional; NITI Aayog called statutory; the Finance Commission called statutory.

What is the remedy?
column2: Rehearse three lists, not individual bodies. | Pedigree | Members | |---|---| | Constitutional | Election Commission, Finance Commission, CAG, UPSC and State PSCs, Attorney General, National Commission for SCs and STs | | Statutory | NHRC, CVC, CIC, National Commission for Women, SEBI, RBI, NGT, ESIC, and EPFO's Central Board of Trustees — now under the Code on Social Security | | Executive / non-statutory | NITI Aayog, the erstwhile Planning Commission, most Cabinet Committees |

column1:
T-13 The plausible-but-nonexistent entity ★★★☆☆

A scheme, committee or body that sounds entirely reasonable and does not exist, or that conflates two real names.

What is the remedy?
column2: Invert the default, carefully. If you have prepared the scheme landscape and a name is wholly unfamiliar, that is weak evidence of fabrication rather than evidence of your own gap. Weak. Combine it with the other options; never decide on it alone, because the mirror error is T-26. pagebreak

column1:
T-14 True statement, false reason ★★★★★

Assertion-Reason, or a composite X happens because Y. Assertion true, Reason true, and the Reason does not explain the Assertion.

What is the remedy?
column2: A fixed order, never varied. One: is A true? Two: is R true? Three — only if both are true — does R, by itself, produce A? Most candidates collapse steps two and three. Force the pause. Note that both true, R does not explain A is the correct answer far more often than candidates select it.

column1:
T-15 Reversed causation ★★★★☆

A genuine relationship stated backwards — a rise in the repo rate increases money supply.

What is the remedy?
column2: State the mechanism in your own words, in one clause, before judging. If you cannot articulate the mechanism you cannot evaluate the direction, and the option is unresolved, not plausible.

column1:
T-16 Necessary confused with sufficient ★★★★★

A necessary condition presented as sufficient. Completion of five years of continuous service entitles an employee to gratuity — ignoring that death and disablement waive the requirement, and that entitlement also needs the establishment to be covered.

What is the remedy?
column2: Two separate questions of every conditional option: is this condition required, and is it enough? Statutory eligibility is almost always conjunctive plus provisos, so enough is usually false.

column1:
T-17 The and / or switch ★★★★★

One conjunction changed. A statutory test reading or rendered as and, or the reverse.

What is the remedy?
column2: In any statutory or definitional option, physically mark every and, or and not. Those three words carry more trap density per character than any content word in the paper.

column1:
T-18 Superset for subset ★★★★☆

All claimed where only some is true; a general rule asserted without its carve-out.

What is the remedy?
column2: For every universal claim about a statute, actively recall the exemption provision. Indian labour statutes essentially all have one. If you can name it, the universal claim is false.

column1:
T-19 Chronology traps ★★★★☆

Ordering questions, or a stem asserting that one event preceded another.

What is the remedy?
column2: Do not memorise sequences — memorise anchor years and interpolate. And see §7.3: on an ordering question, identify only the earliest and latest events, which you almost certainly know, then discard every option inconsistent with both. That usually resolves the question without the middle terms.

column1:
T-20 The relative-magnitude trap ★★★☆☆

A comparison between two quantities you both know but have never compared.

What is the remedy?
column2: Whenever you learn two comparable quantities, record the ordering as a separate fact. Fiscal deficit exceeds revenue deficit exceeds primary deficit is not derivable at speed from the definitions alone. Store it as its own line.

column1:
T-21 The definitional near-synonym ★★★★★

Two terms that ordinary language treats as synonyms and the statute or standard does not. Layoff and retrenchment. Provision and reserve. Devaluation and depreciation.

What is the remedy?
column2: §6 exists for this and only this. For each pair, hold one discriminating sentence that mentions both — not two definitions.

column1:
T-22 The partially-true composite option ★★★★☆

A long option whose first clause is unambiguously correct and whose later clause is wrong.

What is the remedy?
column2: Read every option to its final word, then re-read the tail. Trap clauses cluster at the end of long options, because that is where attention is weakest.

column1:
T-23 The overqualified true statement ★★★★☆

A true statement made false by an added specific — the right provision with the wrong commencement date, the right scheme with the wrong ministry, the right committee with the wrong chair.

What is the remedy?
column2: Decompose into atomic claims and verify each. One false atom falsifies the option, however many true atoms accompany it. pagebreak

column1:
T-24 Anchoring on the first plausible option ★★★★★

Option (a) is plausible, you mark it, and (c) and (d) are never genuinely evaluated.

What is the remedy?
column2: Mechanical, no exceptions: read all four options before marking anything, even when (a) feels certain. Three seconds, and the highest-return three seconds in the paper.

column1:
T-25 The familiarity illusion ★★★★★

A question closely resembling one you have solved, with one word altered. You recall the answer instead of solving the question.

What is the remedy?
column2: Treat familiarity as a warning, not a gift, and re-read the stem word by word hunting the alteration. This is the explicit form of F11.1 §1.2's instruction to leave a question when you feel actively pulled towards a familiar-looking option: in a UPSC paper, familiarity is very often engineered.

column1:
T-26 Over-elimination on partial knowledge ★★★★★

You eliminate the correct option because one component is unfamiliar, reading unfamiliarity as falsity. It feels like rigour.

What is the remedy?
column2: The hard / soft distinction from §1.2, applied consciously. Only hard eliminations move your probability. Soft-eliminated options stay in the pool.

column1:
T-27 The sunk-cost question ★★★★☆

Four minutes spent, and leaving now feels like wasting them.

What is the remedy?
column2: A hard ninety-second ceiling in the second pass, enforced by the clock at fixed question counts rather than by feel. The four minutes are already spent; the only live question is whether to spend more. Mark and move.

column1:
T-28 Bilingual ambiguity ★★★☆☆

Specific to this paper. The Hindi and English texts occasionally diverge in precision, particularly for legal and accounting terms of art.

What is the remedy?
column2: Pick one primary language and read the other only when the primary is ambiguous — cross-reading everything burns time you do not have. For statutory questions prefer the English reading, the English text of Indian statutes generally being operative. Note the question number if a genuine discrepancy exists.

column1:
T-29 Panic-driven pattern hunting ★★★★☆

You notice you have marked (c) six times running and change one.

What is the remedy?
column2: A hard prohibition: never let the distribution of your own previous answers influence a current answer. In the moment it will feel like insight. Note that F11.2's key is deliberately balanced at exactly 30/30/30/30 precisely so that there is no letter to fall back on.

column1:
T-30 The OMR drift ★★★★★

Not a knowledge trap, and the most expensive one in the paper. A skipped question is bubbled in the skipped row, and every subsequent answer shifts by one.

What is the remedy?
column2: Bubble in blocks of ten — never question-by-question, never all at the end. At each block boundary verify that the booklet question number and the OMR row number agree. In the final five minutes check only the first bubble of each block of ten: twelve checks, not a hundred and twenty, and a drift shows up immediately. ::: important | IMPORTANT · T-30 OUTRANKS EVERY CONTENT CHAPTER IN THIS MANUAL A single undetected row shift can cost forty marks or more. That exceeds the entire planning weight of several modules. It is also the only trap in this catalogue with a complete remedy — the procedure above eliminates it, not merely reduces it. Rehearse the block-of-ten audit in every mock from F11.2 onward, under F11.3 §1.1 conditions, until it costs you no conscious attention. ::: pagebreak
